summary: Defines EAP-FAST, an Extensible Authentication Protocol method that sets up a TLS-protected tunnel between a peer and a server and authenticates both sides. Inside the tunnel it carries authentication data in type-length-value objects. This memo is informational, describing a vendor-originated method rather than an IETF standard.

plainLanguage.summary: Two sides build a locked tunnel before they share any secret proof, so nobody outside can see it. EAP-FAST builds that tunnel and then lets a simple password count as proof inside it.

questions: what is a pac in eap-fast
subtitle: An EAP method that builds a TLS tunnel first, then authenticates the user safely inside it.

tldr.problem: Network access needs strong mutual authentication that still works with weak credentials such as passwords, resists eavesdropping and man-in-the-middle attacks, and is light enough for wireless devices.
tldr.mechanism: EAP-FAST first sets up a mutually authenticated TLS tunnel, which a saved credential can resume quickly, then runs inner authentication and TLV messages inside that tunnel and ties them to it with a Crypto-Binding TLV.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational RFC, not a standard, and it has been updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9427.

today: RFC 4851 is an Informational RFC with no obsoleting RFC, and it is updated by RFC 8996 and RFC 9427. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: What EAP-FAST Is For
sections.content:
EAP-FAST (Flexible Authentication via Secure Tunneling) is an Extensible Authentication Protocol method. It works in two steps: establish a Transport Layer Security (TLS) tunnel over TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246), TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) or a successor, then exchange type-length-value (TLV) objects inside the tunnel to authenticate further.

Its stated design goals are mutual authentication, immunity to passive dictionary attacks, immunity to man-in-the-middle attacks, flexibility to support most password interfaces (the RFC names MS-CHAP, LDAP and one-time passwords), and efficiency for wireless peers with limited computing power and battery. Secondary goals are flexibility to extend what happens inside the tunnel and little per-user state on the authentication server.

The state-saving device is the Protected Access Credential (PAC): a shared secret plus an opaque element the peer presents later, based on the TLS session ticket extension of RFC 4507.
sections.plainLanguage: The aim is a login that stays safe even when the password is weak. The server also hands the device a pass, so a later visit is faster and the server does not have to remember everyone.

sections.title: Architecture and Layering
sections.content:
Four logical entities take part: the peer, the authenticator, the EAP-FAST server and the inner method server. They may be separate or combined. In a typical 802.11 setup the authenticator sits in an access point, while a RADIUS server may act as both the EAP-FAST server and the inner method server.

The protocols are layered. EAP-FAST packets travel inside EAP, which needs a carrier such as EAP over LAN, RADIUS or Diameter. EAP-FAST packets carry TLS, TLS carries a TLV layer, and the TLV layer carries an inner EAP method or other TLV information. Everything said inside the protected tunnel has to be wrapped in TLVs.
sections.plainLanguage: It is envelopes inside envelopes. The outer one reaches the right office, the next one is locked, and the secret note sits in the innermost envelope.

sections.title: Phase 1 Tunnel and Phase 2 Authentication
sections.content:
The conversation has two phases. In Phase 1 the TLS handshake gives an authenticated key exchange and a protected tunnel. The server begins with an EAP-FAST Start packet carrying the version and an authority identity (A-ID), which hints which credential the peer should use. This is EAP-FAST version 1, and implementations must set the version field to 1. Implementations must support three TLS ciphersuites, among them TLS_RSA_WITH_AES_128_CBC_SHA (RFC 3268).

A peer that holds a valid PAC puts the PAC-Opaque in the TLS SessionTicket extension of its ClientHello and completes an abbreviated handshake. The PAC-Key is a 32-octet key from which the TLS master secret is derived. If resumption fails, the server can fall back to a full handshake.

In Phase 2 peer and server exchange TLVs, optionally running one or more inner EAP methods in sequence, one after another and never in parallel. Phase 2 must not happen if the Phase 1 handshake fails, and it must end with a protected Result TLV exchange. The tunnel then closes and a clear text EAP-Success or EAP-Failure is sent.

EAP messages can be larger than the medium allows, so EAP-FAST adds fragmentation with L, M and S flag bits and a four-octet TLS Message Length field. Each fragment is acknowledged with an empty response.
sections.plainLanguage: Step one builds the locked tunnel. Step two proves who you are inside it. At the end the tunnel closes and a simple yes-or-no message tells the outside world whether you got in.

sections.title: Packets and TLVs
sections.content:
An EAP-FAST packet carries the EAP Code (1 Request, 2 Response), Identifier and Length fields, then Type 43, a Flags field, a version, and an optional four-octet Message Length that appears only when the L bit is set. The Data field holds an encapsulated TLS record, or the A-ID in a Start message.

Inside the tunnel each TLV begins with a Mandatory bit, a Reserved bit, a 14-bit TLV type and a 16-bit length. If a peer or server does not support a mandatory TLV, it must send a NAK TLV and ignore the rest; an unsupported optional TLV may simply be ignored. Five TLVs are required for conformance, and the RFC says conforming implementations must support seven: Result, NAK, Error, EAP-Payload, Intermediate-Result, Crypto-Binding and Request-Action.

The Crypto-Binding TLV proves that both sides took part in both the tunnel setup and the inner authentications, and it also confirms the negotiated version. It carries a 32-octet nonce and a 20-octet Compound MAC. The Error TLV uses codes 2001 (Tunnel_Compromise_Error) and 2002 (Unexpected_TLVs_Exchanged).
sections.plainLanguage: Every small message inside the tunnel carries a label saying what it is and how long it is. If a label is marked must-understand and you do not, you say so instead of guessing.

sections.title: Key Derivation and Crypto-Binding
sections.content:
The tunnel key block is made as in TLS, with an extra 40 octets called the session_key_seed. When a PAC is used, the TLS master secret is computed from the PAC-Key with a function called T-PRF, built on HMAC-SHA1 and producing 20 octets per block.

After each successful inner EAP method an Intermediate Compound Key (IMCK) is derived from the previous seed and the inner method's Master Session Key, truncated or zero-padded to 32 octets. The Compound MAC in the Crypto-Binding TLV is HMAC-SHA1 over the TLV with the compound key. The final MSK and EMSK are 64 octets each, derived from the last S-IMCK; if no inner method succeeded they come directly from the session_key_seed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each time you pass a check, the tunnel's secret code is mixed again with a new ingredient. That way nobody could swap in a different person partway through.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The design targets wireless media, where anyone can capture traffic. Confidentiality and integrity come from TLS, and the Crypto-Binding TLV ties the inner method endpoints to the tunnel endpoints. The protected Result TLV is the true success or failure indicator, and a peer should silently discard a clear text EAP Success or Failure that disagrees with it.

Method negotiation outside a tunnel is unprotected, so NAK packets can be spoofed to push toward weaker methods such as EAP-MD5, and the RFC advises a policy that prevents negotiating down. It does not recommend separating the Phase 1 and Phase 2 servers, because that can lose identity protection, permit offline dictionary attacks and weaken policy enforcement. The initial identity response is sent in clear text, so no intermediary should trust it. A PAC may be bound to a user identity, and a compliant implementation must validate it against the Phase 2 identities. The RFC also notes that denial of service by bad traffic remains possible.
sections.plainLanguage: The tunnel keeps eavesdroppers out, but the name called out at the front door is still public. So nobody should trust that name until it is proven inside the tunnel.
